doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: Legacy and teaching materials on Finale
summary: He hopes to be remembered for his concept; he keeps studies on Finale and Band in a Box, in transposed parts.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: To wrap up, if you had the opportunity — let’s say an author was doing a jazz biography book and he wanted to do a piece on you, sort of like the Encyclopedia of Jazz, what would you like to see written about your own playing? You see descriptions of people’s playing and I’m wondering if there’s something that would please you if it was written?

Well it might be that maybe perhaps I would be able to do something different that they can enjoy it and they can be just as concerned in the way I was, like with Trane. I mean there are so many great players right now even as well. But I try to keep myself in a position where I’m able to even enjoy myself and play some of the things that are through my concept as I stated, the, as I say, some of the things I’m creating over here and trying to teach. I mean if you see my laptop over here it’s loaded with all the studies. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
Things that you’ve written down and that you’ve worked out in your head and then you’ve written them down for other people to use.

They’re all on Finale, they’re all on BandBox, Band in a Box actually, and I have another program with better sounds. I have all — I have all of the soloists that have performed all the tunes that I have in there and also I have many of the Lennie Tristano tunes, I have about 20 or 25, and I write them all and I write them all in concert alto and tenor, where many teachers only give you a concert part and they say, “Go ahead and play jazz.”
If I saw a concert part with chords it takes away — it takes away from me actually. You know I’ve got to remember what the chord was and I’ve got to transpose it, and then I’ve got to play.
Yeah, that’s a big added step.
It is. I’m telling you that’s it. Especially, I mean look I can transpose alto parts but if I had to really transpose alto chords, never. Never.
